identity.title: Improved Regret Analysis in Gaussian Process Bandits: Optimality for Noiseless Reward, RKHS norm, and Non-Stationary Variance

problem.claim: The paper studies GP bandits: minimizing regret when the unknown reward lies in an RKHS.

gap.claim: The authors identify room to improve maximum-posterior-variance bounds, particularly their dependence on noise-variance parameters, which matters for analyzing near-optimal algorithms.

contributions.claim: A new upper bound for maximum posterior variance with improved dependence on noise-variance parameters.
Refined MVR and PE algorithms with nearly optimal regret in the noiseless setting and regret bounds optimal in RKHS-norm dependence.
An analysis of GP bandits with time-varying noise variance, yielding variance-dependent regret bounds for MVR- and PE-based algorithms.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors state a new maximum-posterior-variance upper bound and use it to refine MVR and PE across noiseless, RKHS-norm, and time-varying-variance settings.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that refined MVR and PE achieve a nearly optimal regret upper bound in the noiseless setting.
The authors report regret upper bounds optimal with respect to the RKHS norm of the reward function.
Under time-varying noise variance, the authors report variance-dependent regret upper bounds for MVR- and PE-based algorithms that match their regret lower bound.

narrative_sequence.summary: Defines GP bandits as regret minimization with an unknown RKHS reward.
Highlights maximum posterior variance as central to analyzing MVR and PE, then introduces an improved noise-variance-dependent upper bound.
Uses the bound to refine MVR and PE for nearly optimal noiseless regret and RKHS-norm-optimal regret dependence.
Extends the analysis to time-varying noise variance and reports bounds matching a regret lower bound.

source_observation.claim: The abstract introduces a central variance bound before listing several algorithmic and setting-specific consequences.

lessons.interpretation: A shared technical result can organize multiple claims while making their dependency explicit.
lessons.application: Present a paper's main lemma or bound first, then map each downstream guarantee to that result and state the setting-specific qualification.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the results do not genuinely share a common technical dependency.

unknowns: The abstract does not provide explicit regret rates, kernel assumptions, horizon dependence, or the precise noise-variance dependence.
The meanings of “nearly optimal” and “optimal” are not quantified, and details of the matching lower bound are omitted.
